section.title: Gethsemane, Arrest, and Peter's Denial
section.sectionRationale: The night of anguish and abandonment. In Gethsemane Jesus wrestles in prayer with the horror of the cup He must drink, surrendering His will to the Father while His disciples sleep. He is betrayed with a kiss, arrested, and deserted by all. Before the Sanhedrin He confesses openly that He is the Christ, the Son of Man who will come in glory, and is condemned. Meanwhile Peter, in the courtyard, denies Him three times and weeps bitterly.
section.thesis: Facing the cup of God's judgment, Jesus submits His will to the Father and goes willingly to arrest, false trial, and condemnation, confessing His true identity even as He is betrayed, deserted, and denied, so that the sinless Son bears the collapse of every human loyalty around Him.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the agony in Gethsemane; the betrayal and arrest; the trial before the Sanhedrin and the good confession; and Peter's threefold denial.

units.label: The agony in Gethsemane
units.note: not what I will, but what You will

verses.text: Then they came to a place called Gethsemane, and Jesus told His disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took with Him Peter, James, and John, and began to be deeply troubled and distressed.
Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep {{gregoreo|watch}}.”
Going a little farther, He fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour would pass from Him.
“{{abba|Abba}}, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this {{poterion|cup}} from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”
Then Jesus returned and found them sleeping. “Simon, are you asleep?” He asked. “Were you not able to keep watch for one hour?
Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.”
Again He went away and prayed, saying the same thing.
And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. And they did not know what to answer Him.
When Jesus returned the third time, He said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? That is enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
Rise, let us go. See, My betrayer is approaching!”

units.label: The betrayal and arrest
units.note: the one I kiss is the man

verses.text: While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders.
Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.”
Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Rabbi!” and kissed Him.
Then the men seized Jesus and arrested Him.
And one of the bystanders drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear.
Jesus asked the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw?
Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.”
Then everyone deserted Him and fled.
One young man who had been following Jesus was wearing a linen cloth around his body. They caught hold of him,
but he pulled free of the linen cloth and ran away naked.

units.label: The trial and the good confession
units.note: I am, and you will see the Son of Man

verses.text: They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled.
Peter followed Him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he sat with the officers and warmed himself by the fire.
Now the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking testimony against Jesus to put Him to death, but they did not find any.
For many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent.
Then some men stood up and testified falsely against Him:
“We heard Him say, ‘I will destroy this man-made temple, and in three days I will build another that is made without hands.’”
But even their testimony was inconsistent.
So the high priest stood up before them and questioned Jesus, “Have You no answer? What are these men testifying against You?”
But Jesus remained silent and made no reply. Again the high priest questioned Him, “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?”
“{{egoeimi|I am}},” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”
At this, the high priest tore his clothes and declared, “Why do we need any more witnesses?
You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” And they all condemned Him as deserving of death.
Then some of them began to spit on Him. They blindfolded Him, struck Him with their fists, and said to Him, “Prophesy!” And the officers received Him with slaps in His face.
While Peter was in the courtyard below, one of the servant girls of the high priest came down
and saw him warming himself there. She looked at Peter and said, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.”
But he denied it. “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about,” he said. Then he went out to the gateway, and the rooster crowed.
There the servant girl saw him and again said to those standing nearby, “This man is one of them.”
But he denied it again. After a little while, those standing nearby said once more to Peter, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.”
But he began to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!”

And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Then Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” And he broke down and wept.

gregoreo.gloss: To stay awake, be alert, keep watch. Jesus asks the three to watch with Him and to watch and pray against temptation, but they sleep. The failure to keep watch in the garden foreshadows their collapse when the hour of trial comes, a warning He had pressed in the Olivet Discourse.

abba.gloss: Father, the intimate Aramaic word a child uses. Jesus prays Abba, Father, in the deepest anguish, showing that even at the edge of the cross He rests in the Father's love. Believers, adopted in Christ, are given the same cry by the Spirit, Romans 8:15.

poterion.gloss: A cup. In the prophets the cup is the cup of God's wrath and judgment. The cup Jesus shrinks from yet accepts is the cup of divine judgment against sin, which He will drink to the dregs in His people's place at the cross.

egoeimi.gloss: I am. Asked directly whether He is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, Jesus answers plainly, I am, and adds the vision of the Son of Man at God's right hand. It is both a claim to be the Messiah and, echoing the divine name and Daniel 7, a claim to divine glory.

basic.context: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus is overwhelmed with sorrow. He falls to the ground and prays that, if possible, the cup might pass, yet surrenders: not what I will, but what You will. Three times He returns to find Peter, James, and John asleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd and betrays Jesus with a kiss; Jesus is arrested, a bystander cuts off a servant's ear, and all the disciples flee, one even leaving his garment to escape naked. Jesus is taken to the high priest, where false witnesses fail to agree. When directly asked if He is the Christ, He answers, I am, and speaks of the Son of Man coming in glory. The council condemns Him for blasphemy and abuses Him. Outside, Peter denies knowing Jesus three times, then hears the rooster, remembers Jesus' words, and weeps.
basic.hermeneutics: Gethsemane shows the real cost of the cross: not merely physical pain but the cup of God's judgment, which makes even the sinless Son recoil, yet He submits. The scene of desertion, betrayal, and denial surrounds Jesus with human failure, so that His faithfulness stands alone. His confession before the Sanhedrin is the clear, public claim to be the Christ and the divine Son of Man, the very truth for which He is condemned.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus asks the three to gregoreo, keep watch, but they sleep. He prays abba, Father, that the poterion, the cup, might pass, yet yields to the Father's will. Before the council He confesses egoeimi, I am, the Christ and Son of Man.
basic.typology: The cup Jesus drinks is the cup of God's wrath in the prophets. The struck Shepherd is deserted by the scattered sheep, fulfilling Zechariah. The silent, falsely accused sufferer fulfils the servant of Isaiah 53.
basic.christ: Jesus is the obedient Son who drinks the cup of judgment, the Christ and the Son of Man of Daniel 7, and the faithful witness who confesses the truth even unto death. He stands firm where all others fail.
basic.god: The Father's will is that the Son drink the cup for sinners, and the Son submits in trusting love. God's plan is fulfilled precisely, even through betrayal, false trial, and denial.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 51 and Psalm 75 speak of the cup of wrath. Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man. Isaiah 53 foretells the silent, condemned servant.
basic.oneStory: In the garden the second Adam does what the first did not: He obeys God's will even at the cost of His life, taking up the cup of judgment we deserved. Betrayed, deserted, condemned, and denied, He stands alone as the faithful one, moving toward the cross where He will drink the cup to the dregs so that His failing people may be forgiven and restored, as Peter's tears already hint.

context.literary:
Mark has arranged this night with great care. The chapter alternates between Jesus and Peter, and the two stories are knotted together so that the reader moves back and forth between the high priest's hall and the courtyard below. Peter follows 'at a distance,' verse 54, and is introduced warming himself at the fire before the trial begins. When the council turns on Jesus, the camera cuts away to Peter, and the verdict on Jesus, 'deserving of death,' verse 64, is followed at once by Peter's three denials, verses 66 to 72. Mark lets the two scenes run in parallel. In the high priest's hall, Jesus is asked 'Are You the Christ?' and says 'I am'; in the courtyard, Peter is asked 'You also were with Jesus' and says 'I do not know this man.'

Each of the major scenes has its threefold rhythm. Jesus prays three times and returns three times to find the three disciples asleep, verses 35 to 41. The false witnesses come in waves, 'inconsistent,' verses 56 to 59. Peter denies three times. The pattern of three belongs to storytelling, but here it is made to carry the weight of failure: three prayers answered by three sleeps, three denials answered by three questions on a beach in John 21:15-17.

The passage also has a deliberate tension between speech and silence. Jesus speaks to the Father in Gethsemane, to the crowd at the arrest, and in a single sentence at the trial. In between He is silent before the accusers, verse 61. The only time He breaks His silence is to answer the question that matters: who He is. Everything else, the false testimony, the mockery, the blows, is received without reply. In the courtyard, by contrast, Peter talks too much, and at the end the words of Jesus return to his memory and silence him.
context.historical:
Gethsemane lay on the western slope of the Mount of Olives across the Kidron valley from the temple, a place Jesus went often, and Judas knew where to find Him, John 18:1-2. The name is usually understood to mean an oil press, which suits an olive grove. It was Passover night, with the city crowded, and the garden was a quiet place just outside it.

The arrest party was sent by the chief priests, scribes and elders, and carried swords and clubs. These were Jewish temple officers with an armed crowd, and John adds Roman soldiers, John 18:3. The kiss was the common greeting of a pupil to a teacher, 'Rabbi.' Judas used it as a sign because in the dark and the crowd Jesus needed to be identified. The 'young man' who left his linen cloth and ran away naked, verses 51 and 52, is unnamed. A linen garment worn over the bare body suggests he was roused from bed and followed in haste. Mark alone tells the story.

The trial was held at night in the high priest's house, with the Sanhedrin gathered, which was irregular by later rabbinic rules and a sign of how fast the plot moved. The law required two or more consistent witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15, which is why the inconsistent testimony in verses 56 to 59 sank the case. The charge of blasphemy had its basis in Leviticus 24:16, and tearing the clothes was a custom on hearing blasphemy, though Leviticus 21:10 forbids the high priest to tear his garments in mourning. The courtyard where Peter warmed himself was open to the night air, and the cold explains the fire. Peter's Galilean accent, verse 70, would have marked him out in Jerusalem.
context.canonical:
The scene is told in all four Gospels with different emphases. Matthew and Luke follow Mark's outline, and Luke adds the angel who strengthens Jesus and the sweat like drops of blood, which some early manuscripts omit. John does not describe the agony in the garden but places its content elsewhere: the troubled soul in John 12:27 and the cup in John 18:11, where Jesus tells Peter, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?'

The cup is an Old Testament image of God's judgment. The wicked drink to the dregs from the LORD's hand, Psalm 75:8, Jerusalem has drunk 'the cup of His fury,' Isaiah 51:17, and Jeremiah is told to take 'the cup of the wine of wrath' to the nations, Jeremiah 25:15. Jesus has already used the figure in Mark 10:38-39 when asked by James and John if they could drink it. In Isaiah 51:22 the LORD promises to take the cup from His people, and Jesus' drinking in the garden is the New Testament's answer to how that could be.

The word 'Abba' is carried by Paul into the life of every believer. In Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 believers cry 'Abba, Father' by the Spirit of sonship, which means the Son's prayer in Gethsemane becomes the prayer of His people. Hebrews 5:7-8 looks back on the garden: 'He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears,' and 'learned obedience from what He suffered.'

The false witnesses and the silence echo the psalmists, Psalm 27:12 and 35:11, and Isaiah's servant who was led like a lamb and did not open His mouth, Isaiah 53:7. The spitting and striking recall Isaiah 50:6. Peter's denial and restoration are completed in John 21:15-17, and his later letter says of Christ that when abused He did not retaliate, 1 Peter 2:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wants his readers to see the cost of the cross, and he is unusually frank about it. No other Gospel presents Jesus so openly shaken: 'deeply troubled and distressed,' 'consumed with sorrow to the point of death.' This is intentional. The readers of Mark were people who might themselves face death for the faith, and they needed to know that their Lord had passed through fear before them. He did not feel nothing, and He did not pretend to. He asked, and He yielded.

Mark also wants his readers to see that Jesus goes to the cross freely. He prays 'Your will,' then rises with 'Rise, let us go,' and meets the arrest by naming it as the fulfilment of Scripture, verses 42 and 49. His arrest is not a defeat but the next step in what the Father has appointed. He could have escaped; He chose not to, Matthew 26:53-54.

The third thing Mark wants is honesty about the church. The disciples sleep, run, deny. Mark records it without softening, and the one he exposes most is Peter, who according to early tradition stands behind Mark's account. The point is not to humiliate Peter but to show that the faithful one is Jesus alone, and that the rest of the church, from its first leaders on, stands in grace and not in merit. A reader who has failed will meet in Peter's tears an invitation, and the words of Mark 16:7, 'and Peter,' show that it is answered.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything here is narrative, and most of it describes what should not be copied. Sleeping through the watch, drawing a sword, running away and denying are not recommended. Peter's sword, verse 47, is described, not endorsed; Jesus rebukes the violence in the other Gospels, Matthew 26:52 and John 18:11. The behaviour of the council is not a template for any court.

The model is Jesus. His prayer shows how to bring distress honestly to God: He names the fear, asks for relief, and yields. The shape is 'if it is possible, take this cup,' followed by 'yet not what I will, but what You will.' That is the pattern of Christian prayer in a trial. His instruction to the disciples, 'Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation,' verse 38, is a command to all believers, and the admission that 'the spirit is willing, but the body is weak' is a sober word about the limits of good intentions.

His silence and His confession are not rules for every legal setting. The New Testament shows believers speaking up on other occasions, as Paul does before the courts. What carries forward is the faithfulness: when the truth about Christ is at stake, a disciple confesses it and does not deny it, as Peter should have done.

debates.question: Why was Jesus so distressed in Gethsemane?

views.label: Fear of death itself
views.case: Some read the agony as the natural horror of a man facing a violent death. Jesus is truly human, and Hebrews says He was tempted in every way as we are, Hebrews 4:15. His request that the hour pass fits a human recoil from suffering.

views.label: The cup of God's judgment
views.case: Many hold that the cup is the cup of the wrath of God in the prophets, Isaiah 51:17 and Psalm 75:8, which Jesus will drink in the place of sinners. On this reading what troubles Him is not only the nails but the bearing of sin and the abandonment He will voice on the cross, Mark 15:34, and Paul says God made Him 'to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The Old Testament use of the cup supports this.

views.label: The struggle before the final battle
views.case: A third reading sees Gethsemane as the moment of confrontation with the powers of darkness, the hour of temptation foreshadowed in Mark 1:12-13. The call to 'watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation' suggests that a real test was in progress.

debates.bearing: These are not rivals. A truly human Jesus feels the horror of death, the horror is deepened because the cup is judgment and not simply death, and the whole scene is a spiritual contest in which He wins by obedience. What the text insists is that He prayed 'yet not what I will,' so that whatever the cup contained, He accepted it from the Father's hand.

debates.question: Who is the young man who ran away naked?

views.label: Mark himself
views.case: A very old suggestion holds that the author is describing his own escape, as a signature in the margin. It would explain why only Mark tells the story and why it is so small and personal. It cannot be proved.

views.label: An anonymous disciple, included as a picture of total abandonment
views.case: Others hold that Mark does not name him because he does not matter. He is the last of those who follow Jesus, and when even he flees, in the most shameful way, the desertion of verse 50 is complete. The linen cloth he leaves behind echoes Amos 2:16, where the bravest flee naked.

views.label: A link to the linen cloth of the burial
views.case: A third observation, not a rival, is that the word for linen cloth here is used again of the cloth in which Jesus' body is wrapped, Mark 15:46. Some readers see a pattern of one who leaves his linen behind and one who is wrapped in it, and a young man in a white robe at the empty tomb, Mark 16:5. Mark does not say so.

debates.bearing: The text gives no identification and the story does not depend on one. What it contributes is the sense that no one is left, and that the humiliation of abandonment is complete. Readers should be cautious about building much on the link to Mark 15:46 or 16:5, since Mark does not draw it himself.

study.originalLanguages:
Mark's words for Jesus' state in verse 33 are unusually strong. 'Deeply troubled' is ekthambeo, a verb of shuddering alarm that Mark uses elsewhere of the crowd's amazement and the women's terror at the tomb, so it is not a mild word. 'Distressed' is ademoneo, which carries the sense of anguish and dismay. And in verse 34 He says His soul is perilypos, 'surrounded with grief,' the very adjective the Greek Old Testament uses in the psalmist's question, 'Why are you downcast, O my soul?', Psalm 42:5. The sorrow is described in the words of the psalms of the righteous sufferer, and the phrase 'to the point of death' marks the limit: the grief itself could kill.

The prayer begins with Abba, an Aramaic word for father that Mark preserves in the original and then translates, 'Father.' It is the only time the word is found in the Gospels, and Paul uses it twice for the cry of the Spirit in believers, Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6. It does not mean 'daddy' in a childish sense, but it speaks of an intimate, family address. The prayer is thus not a distant appeal but a son speaking to his father in the dark.

'The hour' in verses 35 and 41 is hora, and Mark has used it of the coming crisis since the discourse, Mark 13:32. Jesus asks that it might pass, and then says that it has come. The 'cup' is poterion, with the Old Testament sense already noted. The shape of the prayer is a conditional wish followed by a yielding: 'if it were possible' is a wish, and 'yet not what I will, but what You will' is its release. 'The spirit is willing, but the body is weak,' verse 38, uses prothymos for willing, eager, and asthenes for weak, 'without strength.' The contrast is between what the disciples want to do and what they are able to do.

The betrayal scene turns on a verb. Judas 'kissed' Jesus, verse 45, with a compound verb, katephilesen, which suggests an emphatic or repeated kiss, and the sign he agreed upon was that 'the One I kiss' would be the man. Jesus asks whether they come out as against a 'robber,' lestes, verse 48, a word for a bandit or armed rebel. The word for 'betrayed,' paradidomi, 'handed over,' is the same one Mark has used since the discourse, and the Son of Man 'is betrayed into the hands of sinners,' verse 41.

At the trial, 'I am,' ego eimi, verse 62, is an unqualified answer to the question 'Are You the Christ?' The same two words can echo the divine self-declaration of Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10-11, though here they simply answer yes. The high priest avoids the divine name by saying 'the Son of the Blessed One.' Jesus answers from Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13, 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.'

Peter 'cursed and swore,' anathematizo and omnyo, verse 71, calling down a curse on himself if he lied. His denial uses arneomai in verse 72's prediction, the same root as the 'deny himself' of Mark 8:34. The final word is a puzzle. The verb behind 'broke down' is epibalon, which may mean he threw himself down, or covered his head, or began, and no translation is certain. What is plain is that he 'wept,' eklaien.

typology.type: The cup of God's wrath, Isaiah 51:17 and Psalm 75:8
typology.fulfillment: In the prophets the cup is what God hands to the wicked and to a rebellious Jerusalem, and what makes them stagger. Isaiah says it will be taken from Jerusalem's hand, Isaiah 51:22. Jesus takes it in Gethsemane and says elsewhere, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11. The correspondence is that He drinks what sinners should drink. The escalation is that no sinner could finish the cup, and He drinks it to the dregs for others, as Paul says, 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The type is not yet fully seen until the cross, where the forsaken cry is heard.

typology.type: The struck Shepherd and scattered sheep, Zechariah 13:7
typology.fulfillment: Jesus had told the disciples they would be scattered, Mark 14:27, and verse 50 shows it come true: 'everyone deserted Him and fled.' The sheep scatter when the shepherd is struck, exactly as the prophet said. In Christ the shepherd is not a martyred leader but the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The type falls short only in the way scattering is the beginning, not the end: the risen Shepherd regathers the flock, Mark 14:28 and 16:7.

typology.type: The silent, falsely accused sufferer, Isaiah 53:7 and Psalm 27:12
typology.fulfillment: The Servant 'did not open His mouth' like a lamb before its shearers, and the psalmist asked not to be handed over to the will of foes, for false witnesses had risen against him. Jesus is silent before the council, verse 61, and false witnesses are brought against Him, verses 56 to 59. Peter later says He 'did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. The escalation is that the silence is not weakness but strength, and He breaks it only to say who He is. The type is fulfilled at His trial and again before Pilate, Mark 15:5.

typology.type: The righteous man betrayed by a close friend, Psalm 55:12-14 and 41:9
typology.fulfillment: David's psalms mourn a companion who shared sweet fellowship and then turned. Jesus is betrayed by one of the Twelve, with a kiss, the sign of friendship. The pattern in Psalm 41:9 is applied to Judas in John 13:18. The correspondence is the pain of betrayal from within the circle of trust, now by one who ate at the same table. It escalates because the betrayed one is not just a king in distress but the Son who is handed over to sinners. The type is fulfilled in Judas, but the pattern also warns every church, since the one who betrays may be near.

typology.type: Adam in the garden and the second Adam in Gethsemane, Genesis 3
typology.fulfillment: In one garden a man took what was forbidden and hid; in another a man prays, 'not what I will, but what You will,' and does not hide, for He says, 'Rise, let us go. See, My betrayer is approaching.' The first Adam was tested amid plenty and failed; the second is tested amid anguish and stands. Paul's pattern in Romans 5:19 is that through one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, and through the obedience of the One the many will be made righteous. The Adam parallel is a theme that the New Testament supports, though Mark does not make it explicit here.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by showing Him as the obedient Son. Everything that troubles Him is spoken in the language of sonship: Abba, Father. He does not rebel and does not coldly submit. He wrestles and surrenders, and the prayer has the shape of a son who trusts his father enough to be honest. Hebrews sees in the scene the process by which the Son 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8, and says that He was heard because of His reverence. The answer to His prayer was not that the cup passed but that He was carried through it, and raised.

It leads to Christ as the one who drinks the cup of judgment. The cup of the prophets is the cup of God's wrath, and Jesus has told James and John that He would drink it, Mark 10:38. Gethsemane is where the cost becomes plain. The sinless Son does not shrink because of a weak will but because He sees what is in the cup: separation from the Father, which is what sin brings. And so He drinks. Peter later wrote that Christ 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23, and Paul wrote that He became sin for us, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

It leads to Christ as the faithful witness. Before the council, He says what He has not said so openly before: 'I am.' The saying costs Him His life, since the high priest at once calls it blasphemy. He joins two Old Testament texts, Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13, to claim a place at God's right hand and a coming with the clouds. This is the man on trial claiming to be the judge. Revelation names Him 'the faithful witness,' Revelation 1:5, and Paul says that He 'made the good confession' before Pilate, 1 Timothy 6:13.

It leads to Christ as the one who stands alone. In this scene the three who were closest to Him sleep, a disciple kisses Him, everyone flees, the council lies, and Peter denies. Every human loyalty breaks. This is how the cross begins, and the isolation is part of the sacrifice: 'I looked for sympathy, but there was none,' Psalm 69:20, as the psalm of the righteous sufferer puts it.

It leads to Christ as the restorer of Peter. The denial is not the end of the story. Jesus had prayed for Peter, Luke 22:32, and the angel's word in Mark 16:7 singles Peter out by name. In John 21 He asks three times, 'Do you love Me?', and three times gives the commission to feed His sheep, John 21:15-17. The Christ who was denied is the Christ who restores.

One caution. Not every detail is a type of Christ, and the young man's linen cloth or Peter's fire should not be forced into code. The passage points to Him by the way He prays, what He says, how He is treated, and the way the New Testament later reads the night.
study.god:
The passage shows a God whose will is good even when it is hard. Jesus prays 'all things are possible for You,' and the Father does not remove the cup. The Father's silence in the garden is not indifference: it is the same love that, as Paul says, 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The mystery is that the Father who loves the Son hands Him over, and the Son who loves the Father submits. Father and Son are united in the purpose.

It shows a God who is sovereign over betrayal and injustice. Jesus says the arrest happens 'that the Scriptures would be fulfilled,' verse 49, and that the Son of Man is betrayed into sinners' hands, verse 41. The Father's plan is not undone by Judas's kiss, the false witnesses, the high priest's robe torn in rage, or the slaps in the face. Yet the guilt of the men is real: they chose, they lied and they struck. The text holds God's plan and human responsibility together, as Acts 2:23 does.

It shows a God who knows human weakness and speaks to it. 'The spirit is willing, but the body is weak' is not an excuse but a description, spoken by one who is patient with weakness and also firm about the need to watch and pray. Peter is not cast out for his failure, though his failure is serious. The God of the passage warns, foretells and then restores.

It shows a God who is just in a way that includes mercy. The cup is a real judgment, and the Son drinks it. God does not wave sin away. Yet He provides the one who bears it. The seriousness of the cup shows how seriously God takes sin, and the willingness of the Son shows how seriously He takes sinners.

It shows a God who is Father and Son in one purpose. The Son prays to the Father; the Father's will is the Son's will in the end; and the Spirit, though not named in the scene, is the one by whom believers cry 'Abba' and so join the Son's own prayer, Galatians 4:6.

For worship, the passage invites us to bring our fear to God honestly and then to yield, trusting that the one who heard the Son 'because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7, hears us too. It also calls for humility, because the night is full of people who loved Jesus and still failed Him, and for gratitude, because the One who was alone that night did it so that we would never face judgment alone.

crossReferences.note: Jerusalem has drunk from the LORD's hand 'the cup of His fury,' draining it to the dregs. This is the background of the cup in Gethsemane, and verse 22 promises that the LORD will take it from His people's hand, which Jesus' drinking makes possible.

A cup is in the LORD's hand, full of foaming wine, and the wicked of the earth drink it to the dregs. It shows what Jesus sees in the cup: the judgment that falls on sin. His prayer 'take this cup from Me' is the cry of one who knows what is in it.

James and John are asked if they can drink the cup that Jesus will drink. The question is answered at Gethsemane, where He drinks it alone, and the two brothers are among those who fall asleep. The two scenes should be read together.

The writer looks back on the garden: loud cries and tears, a prayer heard because of reverence, obedience learned through suffering. It is a New Testament commentary on Gethsemane and shows that the Son's anguish was real and that His obedience was costly.
Believers cry 'Abba, Father' by the Spirit of sonship. The cry that Jesus uttered in the dark is now the cry of all who belong to Him, which means the Son's prayer has become the family's prayer.

Strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered. Mark 14:27 quotes it before the night begins, and verse 50 shows it happen. The fulfilment is precise, which reassures the reader that the disciples' failure was foreseen and is held within God's plan.

The Servant is oppressed and afflicted, yet does not open His mouth, like a lamb led to slaughter. Jesus' silence before the council, verse 61, matches it, and the silence of the Servant becomes a way the church reads the trial.

The righteous sufferer asks not to be handed over to foes, 'for false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence.' The false witnesses of verses 56 to 59 fit the psalm closely. Reading it together shows the trial as another instance of the pattern in the psalms.

The one like a son of man coming with the clouds receives everlasting dominion. Jesus applies the figure to Himself before the council. The same title that He uses of His suffering He uses of His glory, and the council hears both.

The Lord invited to sit at God's right hand. Jesus quoted it in the temple, Mark 12:36, and now uses it before the high priest, 'sitting at the right hand of Power.' The question He asked His opponents about David's Lord is answered by His own claim.

Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day. Some readers see an echo in the young man who runs away without his cloth. It is a plausible link, not a certain one, and it fits the theme of total desertion.

Jesus tells Peter that He could call on more than twelve legions of angels, but then how would the Scriptures be fulfilled? It shows that His arrest was voluntary and it answers the question of why He did not resist.

Three questions on the shore answer three denials in the courtyard. Peter, who said 'I do not know this man,' is asked three times, 'Do you love Me?' and commissioned to feed the flock. It is the sequel that Mark 14:72 leads one to expect.

God made the sinless one to be sin on our behalf, so that we might become the righteousness of God. It names what the cup holds and why Jesus drank it, and it is the doctrinal summary of what Gethsemane anticipates.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture opens in a garden where the first man chose his own will against God's word, and hid. It reaches its turning point in another garden where the last man says, 'Yet not what I will, but what You will.' Everything that went wrong in Eden is answered here. The first Adam grasped at what was forbidden, and the second receives what is given, even when what is given is a cup of judgment. The fall was disobedience, and redemption begins with obedience.

The night also gathers the story of Israel. The sheep are scattered, as Zechariah foretold, and the leaders of God's people condemn the one they were meant to welcome. The shepherd of the people is struck by the shepherds of the people. The temple charge, 'I will destroy this man-made temple,' echoes through the story to the moment of His death, when the veil is torn, Mark 15:38. The covenant people who were supposed to recognise their Messiah hand Him to the Gentiles.

It also sets up what follows. The cup that Jesus drinks is the cup the prophets saw, and the cross is where it will be drained. His confession before the council prepares the title over the cross, 'The King of the Jews,' and His promise that the Son of Man will sit at God's right hand and come on the clouds is answered by the resurrection and the ascension. The disciples' failure prepares the church to understand grace: a Peter who wept and was restored becomes the rock of the early church, strengthening his brothers, Luke 22:32.

The story ends in the new creation, where the cup of wrath is gone and the cup of salvation is held out. Isaiah promised that the cup of staggering would be taken from His people's hands and they would drink from it no more, Isaiah 51:22. Because Jesus drank it, those who believe will not face the judgment it held. In the city of God there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and the Son who prayed in the dark is seen in light. The faithful witness who stood alone in the night will be surrounded by a great crowd from every nation, and no one who loved Him will fall asleep or run away again.

quiz.q: What did Jesus pray in Gethsemane?

options.text: Abba, Father, take this cup from Me, yet not what I will, but what You will.
options.note: Mark 14:36; genuine anguish joined to full submission to the Father's will.

options.text: That He might avoid the cross entirely.
options.note: He asked if the cup could pass, but decisively submitted to the Father's will, not seeking to avoid it.

options.text: That the Father's will be done even at the cost of the cup.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should include His honest plea for the cup to pass if possible.

options.text: That His disciples would be spared any suffering.
options.note: His prayer concerned the cup He must drink and submission to the Father, not sparing the disciples.

quiz.q: What is the cup Jesus shrinks from yet accepts?

options.text: The cup of God's judgment against sin, which He will drink in His people's place.
options.note: In the prophets the cup is divine wrath; Jesus bears it for sinners at the cross.

options.text: Simply the physical pain of crucifixion.
options.note: The physical pain is real, but the cup's dread is bearing God's judgment on sin, far deeper than pain alone.

options.text: The whole ordeal of suffering, shame, and death He must endure.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but its horror lies specifically in bearing God's judgment for sin.

options.text: A test of His courage with no deeper meaning.
options.note: The cup is the cup of God's wrath, not a mere test of nerve.

quiz.q: How did the disciples respond when Jesus was arrested?

options.text: They all deserted Him and fled, one even leaving his garment to escape.
options.note: Mark 14:50-52; the sheep scattered, fulfilling Jesus' word from Zechariah.

options.text: They fought bravely to defend Him.
options.note: One struck with a sword, but then all fled; they did not defend Him.

options.text: They abandoned Him and ran away in fear.
options.note: Correct, but it should note the vivid detail of even the young man fleeing naked, underscoring the total desertion.

options.text: They followed the soldiers quietly to the high priest.
options.note: Only Peter followed at a distance; the rest fled outright.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer the high priest's question whether He was the Christ?

options.text: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at God's right hand and coming with the clouds.
options.note: Mark 14:62; a clear claim to be the Messiah and the divine Son of Man.

options.text: He remained silent and gave no answer.
options.note: He was silent to the false witnesses, but to the direct question He answered plainly, I am.

options.text: He affirmed He was the Christ and the glorious Son of Man.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should include the vivid words about the right hand of Power and the clouds.

options.text: He denied being the Christ to avoid condemnation.
options.note: He openly confessed it, which led to His condemnation for blasphemy.

quiz.q: How did Peter respond when questioned in the courtyard, and what followed?

options.text: He denied Jesus three times, then heard the rooster, remembered Jesus' words, and wept bitterly.
options.note: Mark 14:66-72; denial, then remembrance and tears of repentance.

options.text: He denied Jesus but felt no remorse afterward.
options.note: The opposite; he broke down and wept, a sign of genuine grief and coming restoration.

options.text: He denied Jesus three times and then repented in sorrow.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should note the rooster and his remembering Jesus' specific word.

options.text: He boldly confessed Jesus before the servants.
options.note: He had vowed to, but in fact he denied Him three times.

questions: In deep anguish Jesus still prayed, not what I will, but what You will. Where is God calling you to surrender your will to His, even when it is costly?
The disciples slept when Jesus asked them to watch and pray. What helps or hinders your own watchfulness and prayer in seasons of testing?
Jesus was betrayed, deserted, and denied, yet remained faithful. How does His faithfulness in the face of total abandonment strengthen you?
Jesus confessed the truth about Himself knowing it would cost His life. Where are you tempted to stay silent about Christ to protect yourself?
Peter denied Jesus, then wept, and would later be restored. How does Peter's failure and grief give you hope when you have failed the Lord?

translationNotes.note: Abba is the intimate Aramaic word for Father; Mark preserves Jesus' actual cry. The same cry is given to believers by the Spirit of adoption, Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6.

I am answers the high priest directly; the added words draw on Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13, claiming both messianic kingship and the divine glory of the Son of Man, which the council judged blasphemy.
Some manuscripts omit and the rooster crowed here; either way Jesus' prediction of a denial before the rooster crows twice is precisely fulfilled in verse 72.
